analysis.one_liner: Opens the Fed's instant-payment system to low-cost money transfer companies so families pay less to send money abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in October 2024 with no cosponsors and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Federal Reserve to give nonbank remittance companies — the apps and services immigrants use to send money home — direct access to FedNow, the government-run instant payment system. Millions of workers pay an average of about 6% of every transfer in fees; the bill's premise is that competing providers with access to cheap federal payment rails would push that cost down. It also orders the Fed to report yearly to Congress on remittance cost trends.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrant workers and their families who send money across borders, if competition drives transfer fees below today's average of roughly 6% of each payment.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Federal Reserve to let 'affordable remittance providers' — nonbank companies whose main business is low-cost remittances — use FedNow starting 90 days after enactment.

The bill's findings state digital remittance providers cut the average cost of sending money from 9% to about 6% between roughly 2013 and 2023, and that access to Federal Reserve payment rails could push costs lower still.
Providers must be registered with Treasury's FinCEN or otherwise comply with the Bank Secrecy Act, and be regulated by a state or federal consumer-protection agency, before qualifying.
Requires the Fed to send Congress an annual report on trends in remittance costs.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, banks and established money transfer firms would face new competition from low-cost nonbank rivals using the Fed's rails, potentially cutting into fee revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars the Fed from imposing capital or liquidity requirements on remittance providers that it does not otherwise supervise, beyond what is needed to ensure they settle payments — a safety limit critics of nonbank access to Fed payment systems would point to.

'Affordable remittance provider' is left for the Fed to define within 60 days, and Congress gives only general guidelines, so the term could be drawn narrowly or loosely depending on the Fed's discretion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is concrete and well documented: fees near 6% of every transfer take a real bite out of workers' pay, and cheaper rails have already cut those fees before. The trade-off is that nonbank firms on a federal payment system would face lighter oversight than banks, and the core terms are left to Fed rulemaking, so the safeguards and the savings both depend on how it is written.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 118th Congress, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and the committee never acted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Ritchie Torres of New York introduced the bill on October 25, 2024, with no cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, banks and large money transfer firms kept the payment-access status quo, and families sending remittances kept paying fees near the 6% average the bill cited.

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Affordable Remittance Act and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 118th Congress by Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote or committee action ever showed where members stood; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would give low-cost remittance companies access to FedNow, the Fed's instant-payment rails, letting them compete on speed and price. Their gain comes directly from cheaper, faster transfers for sending families.

industries.industry: Money transfer firms (e.g. Western Union-style services)
industries.note: Nonbank transfer companies today charge fees the bill's own findings put at about 6% of each payment on average. New rivals on government payment rails would pressure those fees downward.

The bill specifically excludes depository institutions from the definition and would open a Fed-run payment system to nonbank competitors, narrowing banks' privileged position on federal payment infrastructure. It does not otherwise change bank rules.
